candidates.title: Show HN: Vibivibi – End-to-end encrypted sharing of Coding Agent sessions
candidates.raw_content: Hi HN, I'm Hongyin. I built Vibivibi ( https://vibivibi.com ) because I kept starting a coding agent session on my laptop and wanting to continue it on a server, or hand it to a colleague. I want an easier way to do it but won’t trust anyone hosting my traces who promises they won’t sell it (market price per coding trace is $50 to $100). What Vibivibi does: a small CLI, `vibi`, finds the sessions your coding agents keep locally (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi), encrypts one on your machine and uploads it. On another machine `vibi pull` puts it back where the agent expects it, so `claude --resume ` just continues. `vibi push` can also send a session to someone else by email. Our service cannot read session content. Each user has a key pair made on their first machine; the private key reaches the server only wrapped with a key derived from an encryption password that never leaves the user's machines. Every session version is encrypted with its own random key, which is then wrapped for each recipient (X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM). The server sees account emails, public keys, machine names, sizes, timestamps, who sent what to whom, and an optional plain-text label. Sending to someone who doesn't have an account yet works too: the sender's client makes a key pair on their behalf, locks it with a random 12-character passphrase, and shows the sender that passphrase to pass on out of band. When the recipient signs up and enrolls a machine, their client unlocks it locally and re-keys the session to their own key. The client is open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/subconscious-systems/vibi-cli The crypto and the schemas of everything the client sends live in one package, so the claims above can be checked against the code. It ships as a single executable, no Node or npm needed: `curl -fsSL https://vibivibi.com/install.sh | sh`, or build it yourself. The server (Next.js on Vercel, Postgres, blob storage) is not open source. Pricing: free for 200 MB of encrypted storage and unlimited sends; Pro is $8/month for 20 GB; Team is $15/seat with an admin view and a "send only inside the team" policy. Honest limitations: - There is no password recovery. Forget the encryption password and the key, and everything encrypted for it, is gone. I'd like to hear where the threat model falls short, and which agents or workflows you'd want supported next. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49965199 Points: 2 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: Show HN: Carve – An open-source Mac agent with a choice of models
candidates.raw_content: Hi HN, I built and open-sourced Carve to handle repetitive work in windows you already use. Choose the window in any Mac app where you want it to work, press Option-D, and watch it do what you want. For example, in the demo I show an example CRM and Carve entering contact details and drafting a follow up. It also has the ability to annotate and explain items on the screen. This runs with your own API keys, and can even support OpenRouter, though OpenAI is the best tested. Experimental adapters also for Bedrock, Azure. No reason it couldn't expand beyond experimental support to support more local models. I built this because I found that Claude and Codex were rather clunky when using computer use, I like having a sleek window that just pops up and shows me what it's doing. Also it has the 3 similar modes (approve plan, step by step manual approval, or act directly mode). Local currently covers browser actions via vision models, computer use support is required for operating other native mac apps. This is an ongoing area of work. I'm seeing a lot of demand for local model support and building out relevant tooling so wanted to contribute. We're just now at the point where models are getting fast and smart enough to make rapid computer use possible. You can take a look at the benchmarks in the repository, Carve currently can rapidly and cheaply handle explaining, summarizing, basic navigation, and extraction. Complex, long horizon tasks are a work in progress, though I'm seeing promising results. Failures resemble patterns, and you can identify patterns and fix them by running evaluations in batches. I'd love any feedback on how well the tool works, what you tried, and any issues that you found. Thank you! Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49965123 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: Show HN: Browsentic Open-source Claude for Chrome alternative for any agent CLI
candidates.raw_content: A personal agent harness lives in your existing browser, connects to your claude-code (or any other major harness codex or cursor-cli...) NOT the SDK API, exposes web-optimized tools to the harness - that's Browsentic. A free, opensource (Apache 2.0) with rich capabilities alternative to Comet, BrowserOS, Browser-use, Claude for Chrome or nanobrowser. The unique architecture of Browsentic makes it different from all other alternatives. It uses a loopback MCP server that spawns claude/codex/OpenCode/Cursor harness in a detached process. You can already guess, it is a bi-directional MCP, you can browse agentic through the browser harness or through any MCP client. Browsentic doesn't require any new browser to install and not limited to chromium, it supports Firefox as well. By default you don't even need CDP to perform core agentic browsing. Capabilities: core accessibilities (50+ compare to nanobrowser only had 20), custom skill, record-replay, schedule-monitoring-notification, resolves captcha autonomously, has it's own memory, voice orb over web-speech API, can sideload custom tools, platform + browser + agent agnostic It is opensource, no API key, no telemetry & local first and actively maintained and yesterday was the first public stable launch (v0.8.0) Currently I'm the only author but every & any contribution or suggestion will be more than welcome :) Source: https://github.com/imshaikot/browsentic Install guide: https://browsentic.com/install Docs: https://browsentic.com/docs Install video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8t4l9Q9BkE Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49964361 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: We’re already starting to see what kind of new jobs AI is creating. AI requires significant technical work and surrounding services to deploy into the economy. This means jobs for AI engineers that build applied AI products sold to (or within) enterprises, FDEs to deploy agents into companies, new services firms for deploying AI, and more. And even the published stats of new jobs undercount all the existing jobs that are transitioning to new areas of AI work in an enterprise. Many prior data, research, and software jobs large enterprises are also being repositioned for working with AI. Every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and even law firm is bringing on more technical talent -or repositioning existing roles- to help with agent deployment in their companies. It’s a lot easier to picture what AI can replace vs. what it creates until it starts happening. Now we’re seeing what this looks like.

candidates.title: DHH is fundamentally right about Rust. For context, Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification (carcinization, technically 🦀) for a while. One of the first projects we migrated was Turborepo, from Go to Rust¹. The migration completed, but the RoI was actually quite controversial internally. While Rust was in our eyes better for low-level OS access, something crucial for a build system like Turbo, the human migration costs were very sustantive. Go is very fast. It's beautifully designed. It's easy to iterate on. We were very conflicted about the migration, because it was *humans* writing the code, *even if we knew Rust was a better choice*. The calculus has now changed. What's "best for humans" is no longer necessarily "best for business". FWIW, it's also quite unlikely that Rust is the end-all-be-all toolchain. I'm quite certain there's greener pasture ahead, because Rust itself was designed before the 'supersonic tsunami' of agents hit. ¹ https​://vercel.com/blog/how-turborepo-is-porting-from-go-to-rust
